evidence.craft: Read src/swe_warmstart/warm.py (61 lines), tests/test_warm.py, experiments/run.py, experiments/figure.py and the three sibling modules it depends on (swe-bootstrap boot.py, swe-decay seq.py, swe-allocate policies.py). Small, readable, deterministic, reuses the earlier policies instead of copying them, and figure.py parses results.txt instead of retyping numbers. Defects: warm.py reaches into three sibling projects by relative sys.path inserts and a star import (warm.py:11-13), so the package that pyproject.toml declares cannot be installed and imported on its own, while the README says 'Pure Python, no dependencies'; run.py opens scores.csv and results.txt without closing them; replications (200), seeds and the bootstrap master seed are hard-coded with no flag to vary them, which is how the seed sensitivity below went unseen.
evidence.claims: Backed: every observed-history number in README lines 14-16 and project.json (recomputed above); the part-2 means, intervals and win shares as printed by run.py for master seed 0; 'identical for K from 0.001 to 10^7' on the observed history (check line in results.txt); scores.csv is a copy; 7 tests; the limitations section (kappa 0.07 value scores, lines as cost, post hoc grid, no multiplicity correction) is candid and verified against swe-value/README.md:9. Not backed: (1) README.md:17 'At 10,000 lines (pass A) greedy-1pull +19.1 (1.3 to 32.7) and thompson-1pull +18.0 (1.7 to 31.0) exclude zero' is an artefact of the bootstrap seed: rerunning the subject's own paired_diffs with master seeds 1-5 gives greedy-1pull lower ends +0.0, +1.3, -2.0, -2.3, -0.7, and with 1,000 histories -1.3 (greedy-1pull) and -1.0 (thompson-1pull); master 0 is also the highest mean of the six (19.1 against 17.5-18.3). (2) README.md:18 'none of the differences between one and two pulls is separated from noise by the bootstrap except at 10,000 lines in pass A' infers a one-vs-two-pull difference from which vs-uniform interval crosses zero (the 'difference in significance is not significant' error); the direct paired one-minus-two-pull difference from the same 200 histories is +6.5 [-5.0, +16.0] (greedy) and +7.4 [-1.3, +18.0] (Thompson) at 10k pass A, so there is no exception. (3) README.md:15 'within 1 to 4 points' is 1.0 and 1.3 points in results.txt. The headline itself (one pull removes the observed-history loss) is backed; the one claim the README presents as statistically separated is not, hence 2.
evidence.fitness: Job: a researcher on the track-allocation programme wants to know whether to drop the two-pulls start before trialling a policy. They get reproducible code, the data and a correct observed-history replay, and the honest reading 'one deterministic order'. They cannot take the resampled result as evidence that one pull beats two: paired, it never separates (all twelve one-minus-two differences have intervals including zero; on resampled histories one pull is ahead even at 20k lines, +3.8 and +4.5 in pass A, unlike the observed-history 'price'). The outcome being optimised is a value score whose two passes agree at kappa 0.07, on 7 arms and 160 projects. Nearest prior work: budget-limited bandits with an explicit exploration phase sized to the budget, Tran-Thanh, Chapman, Munoz de Cote, Rogers and Jennings (2010), 'Epsilon-first policies for budget-limited multi-armed bandits', AAAI, and the follow-up KUBE (Tran-Thanh et al. 2012, AAAI); UCB1's one-pull initialisation (Auer, Cesa-Bianchi and Fischer 2002, Machine Learning 47); for decaying no-replacement arms, rotting bandits (Levine, Crammer and Mannor 2017, NeurIPS). None is cited; the README cites bandits with knapsacks and a Thompson tutorial only. 'Forced exploration is too expensive when the budget is small' is the known epsilon-first trade-off, so the result is an application check, not a new finding, and the swe-allocate KnapsackUCB baseline that already exists in the imported code is not run.
evidence.domain: Against budgeted-bandit practice: replay on one logged order is acknowledged; the block bootstrap with 200 replicates puts only 5 replicates in each 2.5% tail, so percentile endpoints move by 2-4 points between master seeds, larger than the margins the README reads (+1.3, +1.7 over zero); the comparison of interest (one vs two pulls) is never computed paired; no correction for the 7 policies x 3 budgets x 2 passes compared (stated); no regret or oracle-gap framing beyond a myopic hindsight yardstick; the shrinkage rule shrinks each arm toward the running pooled ratio r, so sign(index - r) = sign(V_a - r C_a) does not depend on K and K can only reorder arms that are both above the pool: in the observed replays that happens at 207 of 29,638 decisions (scratchpad/kcheck.py), which is why K 'did nothing'; the README attributes this to the early tie and the data rather than to the rule's structure, though it does decline to generalise. I confirmed K can matter on a hand-made state (V/C = 6/100, 30/1000, 1/2000: K = 0.001 picks x, K = 500 and 10^7 pick y). The PhD bar in research/CLAUDE.md is not met: this is a careful exploratory follow-up inside an internal programme.

defects.what: The only resampled result the README calls separated from noise is a bootstrap-seed artefact and a difference-in-significance inference: the 10k pass A intervals over uniform that 'exclude zero' (+1.3, +1.7 lower ends) cross zero under master seeds 3-5 and with 1,000 histories (-1.3, -1.0), and the directly paired one-minus-two-pull difference is +6.5 [-5.0, +16.0] (greedy) and +7.4 [-1.3, +18.0] (Thompson), so 'except at 10,000 lines in pass A' has no basis.

200 bootstrap replicates (5 per 2.5% tail) with a fixed master seed and no paired policy-vs-policy interval: percentile endpoints move 2-4 points between seeds, more than the margins read in README.md:17; run.py has no option to vary reps or seed.

Nearest prior work not cited: budget-limited bandits that size the exploration phase to the budget (Tran-Thanh et al. 2010 epsilon-first; 2012 KUBE), UCB1's single-pull start (Auer et al. 2002), rotting bandits for decaying no-replacement arms (Levine et al. 2017); the existing KnapsackUCB baseline in the imported swe-allocate code is not run, so the result is not placed against the known exploration-budget trade-off.

Core estimators of both new policies are untested: replacing Thompson1's sampled value-per-line with the sampled value sum, or the shrinkage denominator C_a + K with C_a + 1, leaves all 7 tests green; test_thompson1_runs only asserts value > 20 on a constant toy; no test pins run.py output.

Shrinking toward the running pooled ratio keeps sign(index - r) independent of K, so K can only reorder arms both above the pool (207 of 29,638 observed decisions); the README attributes the K-insensitivity to the first-pull tie and the data instead of this structural property, which makes the K grid a near-vacuous test of 'a prior'.
'within 1 to 4 points' for the pass A 20k start-rule gaps; results.txt gives 1.0 (greedy) and 1.3 (Thompson).

'Pure Python, no dependencies' while warm.py imports three sibling research projects through relative sys.path inserts and a star import; the package pyproject.toml declares does not import once installed.

verdict: A small, careful, reproducible follow-up: run.py and the figure reproduce byte for byte, and an independent re-implementation from the README prose reproduces every deterministic observed-history number exactly (greedy 24/58/134, greedy-1pull 33/58/133, hindsight 42/80/138 in pass A) with uniform inside its reported CIs, so the headline that one forced pull removes the 5,000-line loss on the observed order is right and survives a hard-budget accounting. It does not meet the bar: claims 2 and verification 2. The one resampled result the README presents as separated from noise (10k pass A intervals excluding zero, 'except at 10,000 lines in pass A') is a seed artefact of a 200-replicate bootstrap and a difference-in-significance inference; the paired one-minus-two-pull interval includes zero there and everywhere else. Two of four seeded mutants in the new policies' estimators survive, the budgeted-bandit literature on sizing exploration to the budget (epsilon-first, KUBE) is not cited, and the shrinkage rule's K-insensitivity is structural rather than a finding about the data.
